title: Πατρόκλου πυρά
about: The ghost slips away like smoke, and Achilles wakes to say that something does live on in the house of Hades, though without wits. At dawn Agamemnon sends mules and men up Mount Ida for wood under Meriones, and the Myrmidons arm and carry Patroclus to the place Achilles chose, covering him with their cut hair. Achilles cuts off the fair hair he had kept for the river Spercheius, which his father Peleus had vowed in vain, and lays it in the dead man’s hands. At his word Agamemnon sends the army off to eat and leaves the leaders to build the pyre. Sheep, cattle, jars of honey and oil, four horses, two dogs and twelve Trojan captives are put on it, and Achilles promises Patroclus that Hector will go to the dogs. Aphrodite keeps the dogs off Hector, and Apollo spreads a dark cloud over the body so that the sun will not dry it.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ὠρέξατο χερσὶ φίλῃσιν
οὐδ’ ἔλαβε·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, he reached out with dear hands
and did not take hold;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and reached out with his dear hands, but did not take hold of him;
sentences.n: The part opens on the ghost of Patroclus, who has just ended his speech in the previous part. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then, having spoken’ is the formula for a speaker finishing. ὠρέξατο is the aorist middle of ὀρέγω ‘reach out’, with χερσὶ φίλῃσιν ‘with dear hands’; Achilles is the one reaching, and the object is left unsaid. οὐδ’ ἔλαβε ‘and did not take hold’ is aorist of λαμβάνω. The line begins a paragraph in the edition.

sentences.t:
ψυχὴ δὲ κατὰ χθονὸς ἠΰτε καπνὸς
ᾤχετο τετριγυῖα·
sentences.l:
but the soul, down beneath the earth, like smoke,
went off, gibbering;
sentences.i: but the soul went off beneath the earth like smoke, with a thin cry;
sentences.n: ψυχή is the ghost, the soul that has left the body. κατὰ χθονός with the genitive is ‘down beneath the earth’, and ἠΰτε καπνός ‘like smoke’ is a simile in two words. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone, go off’. τετριγυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of τρίζω ‘squeak, gibber’, a thin, high sound, the noise the dead make.

sentences.t:
ταφὼν δ’ ἀνόρουσεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
χερσί τε συμπλατάγησεν,
sentences.l:
and Achilles, astonished, sprang up,
and with his hands clapped,
sentences.i: Achilles sprang up astonished and clapped his hands,
sentences.n: ταφών is the aorist participle of a verb whose root ταφ- means ‘be astonished’ (the perfect τέθηπα is of the same root), here ‘astonished’. ἀνόρουσεν is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’, and Ἀχιλλεύς is its subject. χερσί τε συμπλατάγησεν is ‘and clapped with his hands’, the aorist of συμπλαταγέω ‘clap together’, a clap of grief and wonder.

sentences.t: ἔπος δ’ ὀλοφυδνὸν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and a word of lament he spoke:
sentences.i: and spoke a word of lament:
sentences.n: ἔπος ὀλοφυδνόν is ‘a word of lament’, the adjective ὀλοφυδνός coming from ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament’. ἔειπεν is a by-form of the aorist εἶπεν ‘said’ (ἔπος and ἔειπεν are of one root). The colon introduces Achilles’ speech, the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ ῥά τίς ἐστι καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι
ψυχὴ καὶ εἴδωλον, ἀτὰρ φρένες οὐκ ἔνι πάμπαν·
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly there is, even in the houses of Hades,
some soul and phantom, but wits are not in it at all;
sentences.i: “Ah, so there is something, even in the house of Hades, a soul and a phantom, but there are no wits in it at all;
sentences.n: Achilles speaks, waking from the dream. ὢ πόποι is the cry ‘Ah’; ἦ ῥά ‘truly then’ gives the sense of a discovery. εἰν is ἐν. εἴδωλον ‘phantom’ is an image of the man, and ψυχή the breath-soul that outlives him. φρένες οὐκ ἔνι πάμπαν is ‘wits are not in it at all’, ἔνι being ἔνεστι ‘is in’. The phrase καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι returns at 23.179 with the same English.

sentences.t:
παννυχίη γάρ μοι Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο
ψυχὴ ἐφεστήκει γοόωσά τε μυρομένη τε,
sentences.l:
for all night long over me the soul of miserable Patroclus
was standing, sobbing and mourning,
sentences.i: for all night long the soul of miserable Patroclus was standing over me, sobbing and mourning,
sentences.n: παννυχίη is an adjective used like an adverb, ‘all night long’, and γάρ explains the discovery just made. Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο is ‘of miserable Patroclus’, a genitive depending on ψυχή in the next line. ἐφεστήκει is the pluperfect of ἐφίστημι, ‘was standing over’ (the pluperfect used as an imperfect, as at 6.373). γοόωσά τε μυρομένη τε ‘sobbing and mourning’ is a pair of feminine participles (γοάω, μύρομαι) agreeing with ψυχή; the pair stands at 6.373 with the same English.

sentences.t: καί μοι ἕκαστ’ ἐπέτελλεν, ἔϊκτο δὲ θέσκελον αὐτῷ.
sentences.l: and each thing it enjoined on me, and was like, marvellously, to himself.”
sentences.i: and it charged me with each thing, and was marvellously like the man himself.”
sentences.n: ἐπέτελλεν is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge’, so Patroclus kept laying charges on him, ἕκαστα ‘each thing’. ἔϊκτο is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’. θέσκελον is an adverb ‘marvellously’; the meaning of θέσκελος is not known, and ‘marvellous’ is the house rendering. αὐτῷ ‘himself’ means the living Patroclus. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῖσι δὲ πᾶσιν ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in them all it aroused a longing for lament.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and it stirred in all of them a longing to weep.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Achilles’ speech and begins a new paragraph. τοῖσι … πᾶσιν is ‘in them all’, the men around him, and ὑφ’ … ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι with its preposition cut off from it, ‘stirred up’. ἵμερον γόοιο is ‘a longing for lament’, the longing to weep. The line stands in odyssey-015 with the same English.

sentences.t:
μυρομένοισι δὲ τοῖσι φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠὼς
ἀμφὶ νέκυν ἐλεεινόν.
sentences.l:
And to them as they wept appeared rose-fingered Dawn
around the pitiable corpse.
sentences.i: And as they wept around the pitiable corpse, rose-fingered Dawn appeared to them.
sentences.n: μυρομένοισι … τοῖσι is a dative participle, ‘to them weeping’, with φάνη, the aorist passive of φαίνω, ‘appeared’. ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς is the stock epithet ‘rose-fingered Dawn’. ἀμφὶ νέκυν ἐλεεινόν ‘around the pitiable corpse’ belongs with the weeping. ἐλεεινόν comes from ἔλεος ‘pity’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
οὐρῆάς τ’ ὄτρυνε καὶ ἀνέρας ἀξέμεν ὕλην
πάντοθεν ἐκ κλισιῶν·
sentences.i: but lord Agamemnon urged mules and men to bring wood from every side out of the huts;
sentences.n: A new scene begins at dawn. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’. οὐρῆας is the accusative plural of οὐρεύς ‘mule’ (the same word as at 1.50), set beside ἀνέρας ‘men’. ὄτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and ἀξέμεν is the epic future infinitive of ἄγω, ‘to bring’. ἐκ κλισιῶν ‘out of the huts’ means out of the camp. The unit ends at the mark in line 112.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἀνὴρ ἐσθλὸς ὀρώρει
Μηριόνης θεράπων ἀγαπήνορος Ἰδομενῆος.
sentences.l:
and over them had arisen a good man,
Meriones, attendant of man-cherishing Idomeneus.
sentences.i: and over them had arisen a good man, Meriones, attendant of Idomeneus, who prized manliness.
sentences.n: ἐπί is an adverb here, ‘over them, in charge’, and ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘had arisen’. ἐσθλός is ‘good’. Μηριόνης is the Cretan, and θεράπων ‘attendant’ is the house word. ἀγαπήνορος, ‘man-cherishing’ (ἀγαπάω ‘cherish’ with ἀνήρ), is a stock epithet whose exact sense is not known; Idomeneus is the Cretan king.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἴσαν ὑλοτόμους πελέκεας ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες
σειράς τ’ εὐπλέκτους·
sentences.l:
And they went, wood-cutting axes in their hands holding
and well-plaited ropes;
sentences.i: They went with wood-cutting axes in their hands, and well-plaited ropes;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the men sent out, and ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. ὑλοτόμους ‘wood-cutting’ goes with πελέκεας ‘axes’ (an epic accusative plural). ἔχοντες ‘holding’ governs both the axes and σειράς ‘ropes’, which are εὐπλέκτους ‘well-plaited’, the cords for binding timber to the mules.

sentences.t: πρὸ δ’ ἄρ’ οὐρῆες κίον αὐτῶν.
sentences.l: and ahead of them went the mules.
sentences.i: and the mules went ahead of them.
sentences.n: πρό is an adverb, ‘ahead’, with αὐτῶν ‘of them’ the men. οὐρῆες ‘mules’ is the nominative plural of οὐρεύς, and κίον is the imperfect of κίω ‘go’. The mules go in front because they will carry the wood back.

sentences.t: πολλὰ δ’ ἄναντα κάταντα πάραντά τε δόχμιά τ’ ἦλθον·
sentences.l: and many ways uphill, downhill, alongside, and aslant they went;
sentences.i: and they went over much ground, uphill and downhill, along and aslant;
sentences.n: The four adjectives are neuter plurals used as adverbs of the way travelled. ἄναντα is ‘uphill’, κάταντα ‘downhill’, δόχμια ‘aslant’. πάραντα is built from the same stem as ἄναντα and κάταντα, and its sense is not certain; ‘alongside, along the level’ is a guess. ἦλθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. The line has only a middle stop (ἦλθον·), not a full one.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ κνημοὺς προσέβαν πολυπίδακος Ἴδης,
αὐτίκ’ ἄρα δρῦς ὑψικόμους ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ
τάμνον ἐπειγόμενοι·
sentences.i: But when they came to the spurs of many-springed Ida, they straightway began to cut high-crowned oaks with long-pointed bronze, pressing on;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ … προσέβαν ‘but when they had come up to’ is a clause with the aorist of προσβαίνω. κνημούς ‘spurs’ are the foot-hills of Ida, and πολυπίδακος ‘many-springed’ is the stock epithet of the mountain (πίδαξ ‘spring’). δρῦς ὑψικόμους is ‘high-crowned oaks’, ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ ‘long-pointed bronze’ the axes. τάμνον is the imperfect of τάμνω (= τέμνω ‘cut’), and ἐπειγόμενοι ‘pressing on, hurrying’ is a middle participle.

sentences.t:
ταὶ δὲ μεγάλα κτυπέουσαι
πῖπτον·
sentences.l:
and they, greatly thundering,
fell;
sentences.i: and the oaks fell, thundering loudly;
sentences.n: ταί is the old demonstrative for the article, feminine plural: ‘they’, the oaks (δρῦς is feminine). κτυπέουσαι is the feminine participle of κτυπέω ‘thunder, resound’ (the house word), and μεγάλα is neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘greatly’. πῖπτον is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fall’.

sentences.t:
τὰς μὲν ἔπειτα διαπλήσσοντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἔκδεον ἡμιόνων·
sentences.l:
and these then, striking them apart, the Achaeans
bound to the mules;
sentences.i: The Achaeans then hacked them apart and bound them to the mules;
sentences.n: τάς is ‘these’, the felled oaks, with Ἀχαιοί the subject. διαπλήσσοντες is a participle of διαπλήσσω ‘strike apart’, probably chopping the trunks into lengths. ἔκδεον is the imperfect of ἐκδέω ‘tie on’, and ἡμιόνων is the genitive of ἡμίονος ‘mule’, the animals that will haul the timber.

sentences.t:
ταὶ δὲ χθόνα ποσσὶ δατεῦντο
ἐλδόμεναι πεδίοιο διὰ ῥωπήϊα πυκνά.
sentences.l:
and they with their feet tore up the ground,
longing for the plain, through thick brushwood.
sentences.i: and the mules tore up the ground with their feet, longing for the plain, through the thick brushwood.
sentences.n: ταί is again the feminine ‘they’, now the mules. δατεῦντο is the imperfect middle of δατέομαι ‘divide, cut up’, so the hooves cut up the ground. ἐλδόμεναι ‘longing’ takes the genitive πεδίοιο ‘for the plain’, the open ground by the ships. ῥωπήϊα is ‘brushwood’, and πυκνά ‘thick’.

sentences.t: πάντες δ’ ὑλοτόμοι φιτροὺς φέρον·
sentences.l: and all the woodcutters carried logs;
sentences.i: All the woodcutters carried logs,
sentences.n: ὑλοτόμοι is the noun ‘woodcutters’, from ὕλη ‘wood’ and τέμνω ‘cut’. φιτρούς are ‘logs’, and φέρον is the imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’. The mark after φέρον is a middle stop: the explanation follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς γὰρ ἀνώγει
Μηριόνης θεράπων ἀγαπήνορος Ἰδομενῆος.
sentences.l:
for so bade
Meriones, attendant of man-cherishing Idomeneus.
sentences.i: for so Meriones, attendant of Idomeneus, who prized manliness, had bidden them.
sentences.n: ὡς γάρ ‘for so’ gives the reason, and ἀνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, used as a past tense. Line 124 is word for word line 113, and its English is the same. The orders came from Meriones, not from Agamemnon, who had only set the work going.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ ἀκτῆς βάλλον ἐπισχερώ,
sentences.l: and down on the headland they threw them one after another,
sentences.i: and they threw them down on the headland one after another,
sentences.n: κάδ is κατά with the final vowel dropped and the τ assimilated to the following δ, an adverb with βάλλον ‘threw down’, the imperfect. ἀκτῆς is the genitive of ἀκτή ‘headland’ (the house word), a projecting stretch of shore. ἐπισχερώ ‘one after another’ is an adverb meaning in a row. The logs are laid out along the shore where the mound will be.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
φράσσατο Πατρόκλῳ μέγα ἠρίον ἠδὲ οἷ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
where Achilles
planned a great mound for Patroclus and for himself.
sentences.i: where Achilles planned a great mound for Patroclus and for himself.
sentences.n: ἔνθα here is the relative ‘where’. φράσσατο is the aorist middle of φράζω ‘plan, devise’, and ἠρίον is ‘a mound’, a grave-mound. Πατρόκλῳ is dative, ‘for Patroclus’, and ἠδὲ οἷ αὐτῷ ‘and for himself’ has οἷ as the reflexive ‘him’, with αὐτῷ added for emphasis. The mound for Achilles himself looks forward to the request of the ghost.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πάντῃ παρακάββαλον ἄσπετον ὕλην
ἥατ’ ἄρ’ αὖθι μένοντες ἀολλέες.
sentences.l:
But when on every side they had thrown down boundless wood,
they were sitting there, waiting, in a close mass.
sentences.i: But when they had thrown down the boundless wood on every side, they sat waiting there in a close mass.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ … παρακάββαλον ‘but when they had thrown down beside’ is the aorist of παρακαταβάλλω (παρὰ κατ-, with the doubled β), πάντῃ ‘on every side’. ἄσπετον ὕλην is ‘boundless wood’; ὕλη is timber for the pyre. ἥατ’ is ἥατο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, with μένοντες ‘waiting’ and αὖθι ‘there’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ is a stock adverbial adjective.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
αὐτίκα Μυρμιδόνεσσι φιλοπτολέμοισι κέλευσε
χαλκὸν ζώννυσθαι,
sentences.l:
but Achilles
at once to the war-loving Myrmidons gave command
to gird on bronze,
sentences.i: but Achilles at once ordered the war-loving Myrmidons to gird on their bronze,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς turns to the leader. Μυρμιδόνεσσι φιλοπτολέμοισι is the dative ‘to the war-loving Myrmidons’, and κέλευσε ‘gave command’ takes two infinitives, the first ζώννυσθαι ‘to gird on’ (middle of ζώννυμι). χαλκόν ‘bronze’ stands for the armour, the metal for the thing made of it.

sentences.t:
ζεῦξαι δ’ ὑπ’ ὄχεσφιν ἕκαστον
ἵππους·
sentences.l:
and to yoke under the chariots each man
his horses;
sentences.i: and each man to yoke his horses to the chariots;
sentences.n: ζεῦξαι is the aorist infinitive of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, the second thing Achilles commanded. ὑπ’ ὄχεσφιν ‘under the chariots’ has the old ending -φιν, a dative plural of ὄχος. ἕκαστον ‘each’ is accusative, in agreement with the unspoken subject of the infinitive, each Myrmidon, and ἵππους is the object, set after the line break.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὄρνυντο καὶ ἐν τεύχεσσιν ἔδυνον,
sentences.l: and they roused themselves and into their arms went,
sentences.i: and they roused themselves and put on their armour,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Myrmidons. ὄρνυντο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, and ἔδυνον the imperfect of δύνω ‘go into’. ἐν τεύχεσσιν ἔδυνον is the Greek idiom for putting on armour, entering into the arms.

sentences.t: ἂν δ’ ἔβαν ἐν δίφροισι παραιβάται ἡνίοχοί τε,
sentences.l: and up on the chariots went the side-riders and the charioteers,
sentences.i: and the fighters at the driver’s side and the charioteers mounted the chariots,
sentences.n: ἂν … ἔβαν is ἀνέβησαν, the preposition set apart from the verb: ‘mounted’. ἐν δίφροισι is ‘onto the chariots’. παραιβάται are the warriors who ride beside the charioteer (παρὰ + βαίνω), and ἡνίοχοι are the charioteers who drive. The two men in each car are named together.

sentences.t:
πρόσθε μὲν ἱππῆες, μετὰ δὲ νέφος εἵπετο πεζῶν
μυρίοι·
sentences.l:
in front the horsemen, and after them followed a cloud of men on foot,
countless;
sentences.i: The horsemen went in front, and after them followed a cloud of men on foot, countless;
sentences.n: πρόσθε μέν is ‘in front’, answered by μετὰ δέ ‘and after’. ἱππῆες are the horsemen, here those who ride in chariots. νέφος πεζῶν is ‘a cloud of men on foot’, with εἵπετο, the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, and μυρίοι ‘countless’. The word is set at the start of the next line.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ μέσοισι φέρον Πάτροκλον ἑταῖροι.
sentences.l: and in the midst his companions carried Patroclus.
sentences.i: and in the midst of them his companions carried Patroclus.
sentences.n: ἐν δὲ μέσοισι is ‘and in the middle’ of the column, with φέρον the imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’. ἑταῖροι ‘companions’ are the men who carry the body, Patroclus’s own comrades.

sentences.t:
θριξὶ δὲ πάντα νέκυν καταείνυσαν, ἃς ἐπέβαλλον
κειρόμενοι·
sentences.l:
and with hair they covered all the corpse, which they threw on,
cutting it off;
sentences.i: They covered the whole corpse with hair, which they threw on it as they cut it off;
sentences.n: θριξί is the dative plural of θρίξ ‘hair’, the means of covering. καταείνυσαν is the imperfect of καταέννυμι ‘cover over’. ἃς ἐπέβαλλον ‘which they threw upon’ has the relative ἅς for the hair. κειρόμενοι is a middle participle of κείρω ‘cut’: they cut off their own hair. Cutting hair for the dead was a sign of mourning.

sentences.t:
ὄπιθεν δὲ κάρη ἔχε δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἀχνύμενος·
sentences.l:
and behind held the head heavenly Achilles,
grieving;
sentences.i: and behind them heavenly Achilles held the head, grieving;
sentences.n: ὄπιθεν is ‘from behind’, the last place in the column. κάρη is ‘head’, and ἔχε the imperfect of ἔχω ‘hold’. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘heavenly Achilles’, the stock phrase, and ἀχνύμενος is ‘grieving’.

sentences.t: ἕταρον γὰρ ἀμύμονα πέμπ’ Ἄϊδος δέ.
sentences.l: for a blameless companion he was sending to Hades.
sentences.i: for he was sending his blameless companion to Hades.
sentences.n: ἕταρον is the epic form of ἑταῖρον ‘companion’, and ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet. πέμπ’ is πέμπε, the imperfect of πέμπω ‘send’: this is the funeral procession itself. Ἄϊδος δέ is ‘to Hades’, with the goal-ending -δε written apart from the genitive. γάρ gives the reason for Achilles’ grief.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε χῶρον ἵκανον ὅθί σφισι πέφραδ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
κάτθεσαν,
sentences.l:
And when they came to the place where Achilles had pointed it out to them,
they set him down,
sentences.i: And when they came to the place Achilles had shown them, they set him down,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. οἳ δ’ ὅτε … ἵκανον ‘and when they came’ is the imperfect of ἱκάνω (= ἱκνέομαι ‘come’). ὅθι is ‘where’, σφισι ‘to them’, and πέφραδ’ is πέφραδε, the reduplicated aorist of φράζω ‘point out’. κάτθεσαν is the unaugmented aorist of κατατίθημι ‘set down’. The object ‘him’ is understood, the dead Patroclus.

sentences.t: αἶψα δέ οἱ μενοεικέα νήεον ὕλην.
sentences.l: and at once for him satisfying wood they heaped up.
sentences.i: and at once they heaped up satisfying wood for him.
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘at once’, and οἱ ‘for him’ refers to Patroclus. μενοεικέα, ‘satisfying’, means as much as the heart (μένος) could wish. νήεον is the imperfect of νηέω ‘heap up’, and ὕλην the ‘wood’ of the pyre. The words νήεον ὕλην return in line 163.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Then in turn another thing devised swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Then swift-footed, heavenly Achilles thought of something else:
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘then’, αὖτε ‘in turn, again’, and ἄλλα ‘another thing’. ἐνόησε is the aorist of νοέω, ‘devise, think of’, as in the formula ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock epithet pair ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’ (the formation of ποδάρκης is uncertain, probably πούς + ἀρκέω). The colon introduces the offering of the hair.

sentences.t:
στὰς ἀπάνευθε πυρῆς ξανθὴν ἀπεκείρατο χαίτην,
τήν ῥα Σπερχειῷ ποταμῷ τρέφε τηλεθόωσαν·
sentences.l:
standing apart from the pyre he cut off his fair hair,
which for the river Spercheius he had been nourishing, thriving;
sentences.i: Standing apart from the pyre, he cut off his fair hair, which he had been growing, thriving as it was, for the river Spercheius;
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘stand’, and ἀπάνευθε πυρῆς is ‘apart from the pyre’. ξανθήν is ‘fair’, the colour of the hair, and ἀπεκείρατο is the aorist middle of ἀποκείρω ‘cut off one’s own’. τήν is the relative ‘which’, and τρέφε the imperfect of τρέφω ‘nourish, let grow’. Spercheius is the river of Achilles’ homeland in Thessaly, and τηλεθόωσαν ‘thriving’ is the participle of τηλεθάω.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπεν ἰδὼν ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον·
sentences.l: and vexed he spoke, looking out over the wine-faced open-sea:
sentences.i: Troubled, he spoke, looking out over the sea that has the look of wine:
sentences.n: ὀχθήσας, the aorist participle of ὀχθέω, is ‘troubled’, the mood of one about to confess a failure. ἰδὼν ἐπί is ‘looking out over’ the sea. οἴνοπα πόντον is ‘the wine-faced open-sea’, οἶνοψ ‘wine-looking’ being the house epithet for the sea. The colon begins the prayer, which is a speech.

sentences.t:
Σπερχεί’ ἄλλως σοί γε πατὴρ ἠρήσατο Πηλεὺς
κεῖσέ με νοστήσαντα φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
σοί τε κόμην κερέειν ῥέξειν θ’ ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην,
sentences.i: “Spercheius, it was in vain that my father Peleus prayed to you that, when I had returned home to my dear native land, I should cut my hair for you and sacrifice a holy hecatomb,
sentences.n: Achilles addresses the river by name: Σπερχεί’ is the vocative of Σπερχειός. ἄλλως is ‘in vain’, and πατήρ is Achilles’ own father, Peleus, who prayed (ἠρήσατο, aorist of ἀράομαι) for his son’s return. The prayer is in indirect form: με νοστήσαντα ‘I, having returned’, with the infinitives κερέειν ‘to cut’ and ῥέξειν ‘to sacrifice’. κεῖσε ‘thither’ points to the homeland, and ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην is ‘a holy hecatomb’.

sentences.t:
πεντήκοντα δ’ ἔνορχα παρ’ αὐτόθι μῆλ’ ἱερεύσειν
ἐς πηγάς, ὅθι τοι τέμενος βωμός τε θυήεις.
sentences.l:
and fifty uncastrated beasts of the flock there beside you to slaughter,
at the springs, where for you is a precinct and a fragrant altar.
sentences.i: and to slaughter fifty uncastrated beasts of the flock there beside you, at the springs, where you have your precinct and a fragrant altar.
sentences.n: The prayer continues with a third infinitive, ἱερεύσειν ‘to slaughter’ (future; the house word, the animals being an offering, as ῥέξειν ‘sacrifice’ is the offering as a whole). ἔνορχα, ‘with their testicles’, means uncastrated males, and μῆλα is the word for sheep and goats together. παρ’ αὐτόθι is ‘there beside you’, and ἐς πηγάς ‘at the springs’ names the place. ὅθι τοι is ‘where for you’, with τέμενος ‘precinct’ and βωμὸς θυήεις ‘fragrant altar’ (θυήεις from θύος ‘incense’).

sentences.t: ὣς ἠρᾶθ’ ὃ γέρων, σὺ δέ οἱ νόον οὐκ ἐτέλεσσας.
sentences.l: So prayed the old man, but you for him did not fulfil his purpose.
sentences.i: So the old man prayed, but you did not fulfil his purpose.
sentences.n: ὣς ἠρᾶθ’ ὃ γέρων is ‘so prayed the old man’, ἠρᾶθ’ being ἠρᾶτο, the imperfect of ἀράομαι, and ὃ γέρων showing the old pronoun on its way to being the article. σὺ δέ ‘but you’ turns to the river, with οἱ ‘for him’. νόον is ‘purpose’, and ἐτέλεσσας is the aorist of τελέω ‘fulfil’, written with σσ for the metre.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ οὐ νέομαί γε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ κόμην ὀπάσαιμι φέρεσθαι.
sentences.l:
But now, since I am not returning to my dear native land,
to Patroclus the hero may I give my hair to carry off.”
sentences.i: But now, since I am not going home to my dear native land, let me give my hair to the hero Patroclus to carry with him.”
sentences.n: The first line stands in iliad-117 (18.101) with the same English. νέομαι is ‘return’, a present that has the sense of a future. ὀπάσαιμι is the aorist optative of ὀπάζω ‘give, bestow’, a wish or resolve, ‘may I give’. Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ is ‘to the hero Patroclus’, and φέρεσθαι is a middle infinitive: ‘to carry away with him’, to the other world. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χερσὶ κόμην ἑτάροιο φίλοιο
θῆκεν, τοῖσι δὲ πᾶσιν ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, in the hands of his dear companion he placed the hair,
and in them all it aroused a longing for lament.
sentences.i: With these words he laid the hair in the hands of his dear companion, and it stirred in all of them a longing to weep.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is the aorist participle of λέγω. ἐν χερσί is ‘in the hands’, ἑτάροιο φίλοιο ‘of the dear companion’, and θῆκεν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘place’. The second line is the same as 23.108, and its English is the same: τοῖσι … πᾶσιν ‘in them all’, ἵμερον γόοιο ‘a longing for lament’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ὀδυρομένοισιν ἔδυ φάος ἠελίοιο
εἰ μὴ Ἀχιλλεὺς αἶψ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι εἶπε παραστάς·
sentences.l:
And indeed, as they lamented, would have set the light of the sun,
if Achilles had not at once spoken to Agamemnon, standing beside him:
sentences.i: And the light of the sun would have gone down on them as they wept, if Achilles had not stood beside Agamemnon and spoken to him at once:
sentences.n: The first line also stands in the Odyssey (16.220), and its English is kept. ὀδυρομένοισιν is ‘to them lamenting’, a dative participle, and ἔδυ the aorist of δύω ‘set’ with κε, a past unreal: ‘would have set’. εἰ μή ‘if not’ with εἶπε, the aorist ‘said’, and παραστάς ‘standing beside’, the aorist participle of παρίστημι. The colon opens Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη, σοὶ γάρ τε μάλιστά γε λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν
πείσονται μύθοισι,
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, for to you above all the people of the Achaeans
will obey in words,
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, for it is to you above all that the army of the Achaeans will obey in word,
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’, here Agamemnon. σοὶ γάρ τε μάλιστά γε is ‘for to you above all’, with σοί placed first for emphasis. λαός ‘people’ is the army, the Achaeans, and πείσονται is the future middle of πείθω, so ‘will obey’, σοί being the person obeyed and μύθοισι ‘in words’. The comma ends the first clause.

sentences.t: γόοιο μὲν ἔστι καὶ ἆσαι,
sentences.l: of lament it is possible also to have one’s fill,
sentences.i: there is time for lament, and for taking one’s fill of it,
sentences.n: γόοιο is the genitive of γόος ‘lament’. μὲν ἔστι ‘it is indeed possible’ is answered by νῦν δέ in the next unit: lament is possible, but now the burial must be seen to. ἆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘satisfy oneself, have enough’ so that καὶ ἆσαι means ‘and to have one’s fill of it’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἀπὸ πυρκαϊῆς σκέδασον καὶ δεῖπνον ἄνωχθι
ὅπλεσθαι·
sentences.l:
but now from the pyre disperse them, and a meal bid
them to prepare;
sentences.i: but now disperse them from the pyre, and tell them to prepare a meal;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ answers γόοιο μέν. σκέδασον is the aorist imperative of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, with ἀπὸ πυρκαϊῆς ‘from the pyre’: ‘disperse them from the pyre’. ἄνωχθι is the perfect imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’. ὅπλεσθαι is the infinitive of ὅπλομαι ‘prepare’, with δεῖπνον ‘a meal’ as object.

sentences.t:
τάδε δ’ ἀμφὶ πονησόμεθ’ οἷσι μάλιστα
κήδεός ἐστι νέκυς·
sentences.l:
and these things we shall toil at, for whom most
the dead man is a matter of concern;
sentences.i: and we shall toil at this, we to whom the dead man is most a concern;
sentences.n: τάδε ‘these things’ means the burial. ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘about the matter’, and πονησόμεθα the future of πονέω ‘toil’. οἷσι μάλιστα … ἐστι is ‘to whom most … there is’, with κήδεός the genitive of κῆδος ‘care, concern’, so ‘is a matter of concern’. νέκυς is ‘the dead man’. Those closest to the dead man are meant, Achilles first among them.

sentences.t: παρὰ δ’ οἵ τ’ ἀγοὶ ἄμμι μενόντων.
sentences.l: and beside us let the leaders stay.”
sentences.i: and let the leaders stay here beside us.”
sentences.n: παρά is an adverb ‘beside’, and ἄμμι is an old form of ἡμῖν ‘to us’. οἵ τ’ ἀγοί is ‘the leaders’, ἀγός from ἄγω ‘lead’. μενόντων is the third plural imperative of μένω ‘stay’, ‘let them stay’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
αὐτίκα λαὸν μὲν σκέδασεν κατὰ νῆας ἐΐσας,
sentences.l:
But when he heard this, lord of men Agamemnon,
at once he dispersed the people among the well-balanced ships,
sentences.i: But when Agamemnon, lord of men, heard this, he at once dispersed the army to the well-balanced ships,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. αὐτὰρ ἐπεί … ἄκουσεν is ‘but when he heard’, with τό γε ‘this’ pointing to Achilles’ speech, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon. λαόν ‘people’ is the army; σκέδασεν is the aorist of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’. νῆας ἐΐσας is ‘well-balanced ships’, the sense of ἐΐσας being not certain.

sentences.t:
κηδεμόνες δὲ παρ’ αὖθι μένον καὶ νήεον ὕλην,
ποίησαν δὲ πυρὴν ἑκατόμπεδον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
sentences.l:
and the caretakers stayed there beside and heaped up wood,
and they made a pyre a hundred feet here and there,
sentences.i: while those in charge of the burial stayed there and heaped up wood, and made a pyre a hundred feet this way and that,
sentences.n: κηδεμόνες, from κῆδος ‘care’, are those in charge of the funeral, the mourners with a duty to the dead. παρ’ … μένον is ‘stayed beside’ (the pyre), with αὖθι ‘there’, and νήεον ‘heaped up’. ποίησαν is the aorist of ποιέω ‘make’, and ἑκατόμπεδον ‘a hundred feet’ is an adjective for the pyre, with ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘here and there’ (‘this way and that’ in the English layer): a pyre a hundred feet on each side.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ πυρῇ ὑπάτῃ νεκρὸν θέσαν ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ.
sentences.l: and on the topmost pyre they set the corpse, grieving in heart.
sentences.i: and on the top of the pyre they laid the corpse, grieving in heart.
sentences.n: ἐν δὲ πυρῇ ὑπάτῃ is ‘and on the topmost part of the pyre’, ὑπάτῃ being the superlative ‘uppermost’. θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set’, and νεκρόν ‘corpse’ the object. ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ ‘grieving in heart’ is an accusative of respect and a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ ἴφια μῆλα καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς
πρόσθε πυρῆς ἔδερόν τε καὶ ἄμφεπον·
sentences.l:
and many stout flocks and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle
in front of the pyre they flayed and were busying themselves about;
sentences.i: They flayed many stout flocks and cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn in front of the pyre, and were busying themselves about them;
sentences.n: The first line also stands in iliad-056 (9.466), with the same English. ἴφια μῆλα is ‘stout flocks’, and εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς ‘cattle rolling-gaited, crumple-horned’. πρόσθε πυρῆς is ‘in front of the pyre’. ἔδερον is the imperfect of δέρω ‘flay’, and ἄμφεπον that of ἀμφέπω, ‘busy oneself about’. The ‘rolling-gaited’ sense of εἰλίπους is the usual explanation.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πάντων
δημὸν ἑλὼν ἐκάλυψε νέκυν μεγάθυμος Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς,
sentences.l:
and from them all
the fat taking he covered the corpse, great-hearted Achilles,
to the feet from the head,
sentences.i: and great-hearted Achilles took the fat from them all and covered the corpse with it from head to foot,
sentences.n: ἐκ … πάντων ‘from all of them’ means from all the slaughtered beasts. δημόν is ‘fat’, and ἑλών the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘taking’. ἐκάλυψε is the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’, with μεγάθυμος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘great-hearted Achilles’. ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς is ‘to the feet from the head’.

sentences.t: περὶ δὲ δρατὰ σώματα νήει.
sentences.l: and round about the flayed bodies he heaped.
sentences.i: and heaped the flayed bodies all around it.
sentences.n: περί is an adverb ‘round about’, and νήει is the contracted imperfect (νήεε → νήει) of νηέω ‘heap up’. δρατά ‘flayed’ is a verbal adjective from δέρω, and σώματα here means dead bodies, the carcasses of the beasts.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει μέλιτος καὶ ἀλείφατος ἀμφιφορῆας
πρὸς λέχεα κλίνων·
sentences.l:
and on it he set amphorae of honey and of ointment,
leaning them against the bier;
sentences.i: On the pyre he set jars of honey and ointment, leaning them against the bier;
sentences.n: ἐν … ἐτίθει is ‘was setting in’, the imperfect of τίθημι with ἐν standing apart from it. μέλιτος καὶ ἀλείφατος ‘of honey and of ointment’ are genitives of material after ἀμφιφορῆας ‘jars’, the two-handled storage jars. πρὸς λέχεα κλίνων is ‘leaning them against the bier’, λέχεα being ‘bed, bier’ in the plural.

sentences.t:
πίσυρας δ’ ἐριαύχενας ἵππους
ἐσσυμένως ἐνέβαλλε πυρῇ μεγάλα στεναχίζων.
sentences.l:
and four strong-necked horses
hurriedly he threw onto the pyre, groaning greatly.
sentences.i: and four strong-necked horses he threw hurriedly onto the pyre, groaning loudly.
sentences.n: πίσυρας is the Aeolic ‘four’, and ἵππους is the noun that follows ἐριαύχενας. ἐριαύχενας ‘strong-necked’ comes from αὐχήν ‘neck’; the force of ἐρι- is not known, and ‘strong’ is the house guess. ἐσσυμένως ‘hurriedly’ is from the participle of σεύομαι ‘rush’, and ἐνέβαλλε is the imperfect of ἐμβάλλω ‘throw in’, with στεναχίζων ‘groaning’.

sentences.t: ἐννέα τῷ γε ἄνακτι τραπεζῆες κύνες ἦσαν,
sentences.l: Nine to that lord dogs of the table there were,
sentences.i: The lord had nine dogs that fed at his table,
sentences.n: τῷ ἄνακτι ‘to that lord’ is Patroclus, with the dative of possession: ‘there were to him’. τραπεζῆες, from τράπεζα ‘table’, are dogs that fed at the table, the house dogs. ἦσαν is the imperfect of εἰμί. The count prepares the next line.

sentences.t: καὶ μὲν τῶν ἐνέβαλλε πυρῇ δύο δειροτομήσας,
sentences.l: and indeed of them he threw onto the pyre two, having cut their throats,
sentences.i: and of these he cut the throats of two and threw them onto the pyre,
sentences.n: καὶ μὲν is ‘and indeed’, and τῶν ‘of them’ is partitive. ἐνέβαλλε is the imperfect of ἐμβάλλω. δειροτομήσας is the aorist participle of δειροτομέω, from δειρή ‘neck’ and τέμνω ‘cut’; whether the throat was cut or the head struck off is not settled.

sentences.t:
δώδεκα δὲ Τρώων μεγαθύμων υἱέας ἐσθλοὺς
χαλκῷ δηϊόων·
sentences.l:
and twelve of the great-hearted Trojans’ good sons
with bronze cutting down;
sentences.i: and twelve good sons of the great-hearted Trojans he threw on, cutting them down with bronze;
sentences.n: The verb ἐνέβαλλε of line 174 is understood: he threw on the pyre twelve young Trojans. Τρώων μεγαθύμων is ‘of the great-hearted Trojans’, and υἱέας ἐσθλούς ‘good sons’, ἐσθλός being ‘good’. δηϊόων is the participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down’. χαλκῷ is the dative of means, ‘with bronze’.

sentences.t: κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ μήδετο ἔργα·
sentences.l: and evil deeds in his wits he devised;
sentences.i: and he was devising evil deeds in his mind;
sentences.n: κακὰ … ἔργα is ‘evil deeds’, the human sacrifice named in the previous unit. φρεσί is a dative plural of φρήν, ‘in the wits’, and μήδετο the imperfect middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’. The poet’s comment is his own judgement of the act, not Achilles’.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ πυρὸς μένος ἧκε σιδήρεον ὄφρα νέμοιτο.
sentences.l: and into it the iron might of fire he sent, that it might feed upon them.
sentences.i: and he sent the iron might of fire into it, that it might consume them.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἧκε is ‘sent in’, the aorist of ἵημι with ἐν apart from it. πυρὸς μένος is ‘the might of fire’, called σιδήρεον ‘iron’ (made of iron, hence unyielding). ὄφρα νέμοιτο is a purpose clause with the optative of νέμομαι, ‘feed upon’ (‘consume’ in the English layer, as at 2.780), the word used of grazing and of fire taking hold.

sentences.t: ᾤμωξέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα, φίλον δ’ ὀνόμηνεν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.l: And he cried out then, and called by name his dear companion:
sentences.i: Then he cried out and called his dear companion by name:
sentences.n: ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out’, the cry of grief. ὀνόμηνεν is the aorist of ὀνομαίνω ‘call by name’. φίλον … ἑταῖρον is ‘his dear companion’. The colon opens Achilles’ last words to Patroclus.

sentences.t: χαῖρέ μοι ὦ Πάτροκλε καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι·
sentences.l: “Be glad, Patroclus, even in the houses of Hades;
sentences.i: “Be glad, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades;
sentences.n: χαῖρε is the imperative ‘be glad’, the greeting of farewell addressed here to the dead. μοι is the dative ‘for my part’. ὦ Πάτροκλε is the vocative. καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι is ‘even in the houses of Hades’, εἰν being ἐν, and the plural δόμοισι meaning the dwelling. The line is the same as 23.19.

sentences.t:
πάντα γὰρ ἤδη τοι τελέω τὰ πάροιθεν ὑπέστην,
δώδεκα μὲν Τρώων μεγαθύμων υἱέας ἐσθλοὺς
τοὺς ἅμα σοὶ πάντας πῦρ ἐσθίει·
sentences.i: for now I am fulfilling for you everything I undertook before: twelve good sons of the great-hearted Trojans, all of whom the fire is eating together with you;
sentences.n: πάντα … τὰ πάροιθεν ὑπέστην is ‘all that I undertook before’, ὑπέστην being the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι; the promise was made at 23.22. δώδεκα … υἱέας ἐσθλούς repeats line 175 and stands in apposition to πάντα, naming what he undertook. τοὺς ἅμα σοὶ πάντας is ‘all of whom together with you’, and ἐσθίει is the present of ἐσθίω, ‘eats’ of the fire. Line 180 ends only in a comma, so the unit runs on to the mark in line 182.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ οὔ τι
δώσω Πριαμίδην πυρὶ δαπτέμεν, ἀλλὰ κύνεσσιν.
sentences.l:
but Hector not at all
will I give, Priam’s-son, to fire to devour, but to dogs.”
sentences.i: but Hector, son of Priam, I shall not give to the fire to devour, but to dogs.”
sentences.n: Ἕκτορα δ’ is the answer to δώδεκα μέν one line before: twelve Trojans to the fire, but Hector not. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’, and δώσω the future of δίδωμι. Πριαμίδην is ‘son of Priam’, a patronymic. δαπτέμεν is the epic infinitive of δάπτω ‘devour’, and κύνεσσιν the dative plural of κύων. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ ἀπειλήσας· τὸν δ’ οὐ κύνες ἀμφεπένοντο,
sentences.l: So he spoke, threatening; but him no dogs were busying themselves about,
sentences.i: So he spoke in threat; but the dogs did not busy themselves about him,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ and the aorist participle ἀπειλήσας ‘threatening’ (ἀπειλέω). τὸν δ’ is ‘but him’, Hector. ἀμφεπένοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀμφιπένομαι (= ἀμφέπω), ‘were busying themselves about’, with the negative οὐ, since the dogs left Hector alone.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ κύνας μὲν ἄλαλκε Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη
ἤματα καὶ νύκτας,
sentences.l:
but the dogs she warded off, the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite,
through days and nights,
sentences.i: but Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, kept the dogs off by day and by night,
sentences.n: ἄλαλκε is the reduplicated aorist of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, with κύνας as its object. Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη is ‘the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite’, and ἤματα καὶ νύκτας is an accusative of time, ‘for days and nights’.

sentences.t:
ῥοδόεντι δὲ χρῖεν ἐλαίῳ
ἀμβροσίῳ, ἵνα μή μιν ἀποδρύφοι ἑλκυστάζων.
sentences.l:
and she anointed him with oil of roses,
ambrosial, that he might not tear him apart, dragging him to and fro.
sentences.i: and anointed him with ambrosial oil of roses, so that Achilles, dragging him about, should not tear him apart.
sentences.n: ῥοδόεντι … ἐλαίῳ is ‘with oil of roses’, and ἀμβροσίῳ ‘ambrosial’, the oil of the gods. χρῖεν is the imperfect of χρίω ‘anoint’. ἵνα μή with the optative ἀποδρύφοι ‘lest he tear apart’ (ἀποδρύπτω ‘tear off’) has Achilles as its unspoken subject. ἑλκυστάζων is a participle of ἑλκυστάζω ‘drag to and fro’, the repeated dragging.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ κυάνεον νέφος ἤγαγε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
οὐρανόθεν πεδίον δέ,
sentences.l:
and over him a dark cloud led Phoebus Apollo
from heaven to the plain,
sentences.i: and Phoebus Apollo brought a dark cloud over him from the sky to the plain,
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘him’, Hector’s body, with ἐπί ‘over’ as an adverb. κυάνεον νέφος is ‘a dark cloud’, κυάνεος ‘dark-blue’. ἤγαγε is the aorist of ἄγω ‘bring’, and Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ‘Phoebus Apollo’ is the god. οὐρανόθεν ‘from heaven’ has the ending -θεν of motion from, and πεδίον δέ ‘to the plain’ the ending -δε of motion to.

sentences.t:
κάλυψε δὲ χῶρον ἅπαντα
ὅσσον ἐπεῖχε νέκυς, μὴ πρὶν μένος ἠελίοιο
σκήλει’ ἀμφὶ περὶ χρόα ἴνεσιν ἠδὲ μέλεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and covered all the place
as much as the corpse took up, lest before then the might of the sun
should dry up the skin round about the sinews and limbs.
sentences.i: and covered all the place that the corpse occupied, lest before then the might of the sun should dry up the skin about its sinews and limbs.
sentences.n: κάλυψε is the aorist ‘covered’, and χῶρον ἅπαντα ‘the whole place’. ὅσσον ἐπεῖχε νέκυς is ‘as much as the corpse took up’. μὴ πρίν is ‘lest before then’, and σκήλει’ is σκήλειε, the optative of σκέλλω ‘dry up’. μένος ἠελίοιο is ‘the might of the sun’. ἀμφὶ περί is ‘all round’, with the datives ἴνεσιν ‘sinews’ and μέλεσσιν ‘limbs’ after ἀμφί; χρόα ‘skin’ is the object. The part ends here.
